catalog_quote: [p. 273] Nivens (2017) compiles data from several sources including his own fieldwork and fieldwork by other linguists, mainly: Jock Hughes (many languages), Benjamin T. Daigle (Batuley, Mariri), and Antoinette Schapper (Ujir). ... Transcriptions of data are adapted to IPA standards, with the following exceptions. The letter ‹y› is used for the palatal glide [j], Tarangan mid-close [e] and [o] are transcribed ‹ê› and ‹ô› (mid-open [ɛ] and [ɔ] are transcribed ‹ɛ› and ‹ɔ›), and unexpected stress is marked by an acute accent. (The normal pattern is penultimate stress, or final stress if the final syllable contains a mid-vowel.) [p. 88] Informed clarifications are extremely helpful, such as the information found in Nivens (2017) that in the comparative Aru data, transcriptions are adapted to IPA standards, with the following exceptions: ... and unexpected stress is marked by an acute accent (the normal pattern is penultimate stress, or final stress if the final syllable contains a mid-vowel).

new_statements.rule_in_words: For all Aru data in Nivens's Proto-Aru database (Ujir included), stress is by default on the penultimate syllable, or on the final syllable when that syllable contains a mid vowel; words deviating from this default are written with an acute accent. In the Ujir forms printed by Grimes & Edwards only three carry the acute (-dʒáŋ, rián, maníʔ, all final stress on a non-mid vowel); the rest are unmarked, i.e. treated as regular penultimate.
new_statements.exceptions: Final stress when the final syllable has a mid vowel (part of the stated default); lexically 'unexpected' stresses marked ad hoc with an acute -- for Ujir: -dʒáŋ 'bite', rián 'ladder', maníʔ 'thin'.
new_statements.domain_note: A transcription convention for citation forms in a comparative wordlist database covering all 14 Aru languages; second-hand (Grimes & Edwards restating Nivens 2017), not a phonological analysis of Ujir. No first-hand Ujir phonology exists in print as far as could be determined.
new_statements.identity_note: Same variety: the Ujir forms in Grimes & Edwards 2026 come from Antoinette Schapper's fieldwork in Ujir village (ujir1237, ISO udj) as compiled in Nivens's 2017 Proto-Aru database. The stress statement, however, is a database-wide default declared for all 14 Aru languages, not a claim made specifically about Ujir; only three printed Ujir forms are flagged as deviating (final stress: -dʒáŋ, rián, maníʔ).

new_statements.quote: In the languages of Aru, stress is not predictable. As a rule, it falls on the penultimate syllable of a root (e.g., Dobel da-ˈtabaj ‘they carry (on shoulder)’), but in around 30% of cases falls on the ultimate syllable (e.g., da-taˈbaj ‘they hit’, Hughes 2000: 135, see also Takata 1992: 40 for Kola; Daigle 2015: 31 for Batuley). Some deviations from this penultimate stress pattern in Aru can be explained historically as a result of desyllabification or loss of the vowel in the final syllable (e.g. Kola ɸaˈnis < PMP *paniki ‘bat’). [p. 570] ... The languages of Aru form a major exception; the base for reduplication is the stressed syllable, but stress can be initial or final. [p. 576]

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with and adds detail to the catalog's penultimate-default reading (Grimes & Edwards 2026 restating the Nivens 2017 database convention, with three acute-marked final-stress Ujir forms -dʒáŋ, rián, maníʔ): the default is penultimate on the root, but the authors classify Aru stress as 'not predictable' with c. 30% final-stress roots, i.e. a lexical/unpredictable TYPE with a penultimate default rather than fixed penultimate stress. This is a group-level (Aru) generalisation whose examples and citations are Dobel, Kola and Batuley; Ujir is not named, so it applies to Ujir only by subgroup membership (Schapper is the Ujir fieldworker, which lends it some weight).
new_statements.rule_in_words: For the Aru languages as a group (Ujir is treated as an Aru language in this chapter, but is not named in the stress section): stress is lexically unpredictable; the majority pattern (the 'rule') is penultimate stress on the root, with roughly 30% of roots stressed on the final syllable; some final-stress cases are explained historically by loss or desyllabification of an original final-syllable vowel. Stress is root-based (affixes do not count, cf. da-ˈtabaj). Reduplication copies the stressed syllable, which may be initial or final.
new_statements.exceptions: About 30% of roots have final rather than penultimate stress; some of these are historically explained by final-vowel loss or desyllabification (Kola ɸaˈnis < *paniki). Evidence cited is from Dobel (Hughes 2000), Kola (Takata 1992) and Batuley (Daigle 2015), not from Ujir. Separately (p. 567) Ujir is noted to have a phonemic vowel-length contrast from compensatory lengthening (PMP *qaləjaw > Proto-Aru *laRaw > Ujir laːu 'sun').
new_statements.identity_note: Schapper & Zobel 2024 treat Ujir as one of the Aru languages (p. 567: phonemic vowel length 'in Ujir and Kola in the Aru islands'), but their stress paragraph (p. 570) is a generalisation over 'the languages of Aru' exemplified by Dobel, Kola and Batuley; Ujir itself is not named there. Collins 1982 (pp. 131-132) describes Ujir as spoken in two villages, Ujir and Samang, in the extreme northwest of Aru, and places it as its own branch of Aru beside Kola and the South branch; the Teor-Kur pages (122-123) concern Teor, a different language.

readall_conflicts: No direct contradiction on placement: everything found points to penultimate stress on the root as the default. The one difference is of type and of scope: the catalog's existing statement ('fixed: penultimate syllable', from Grimes & Edwards 2026 restating the Nivens 2017 database transcription convention, with 3 of 29 Ujir table forms acute-marked as unexpectedly final-stressed) treats penultimate as the rule with marked exceptions, whereas Schapper & Zobel 2024 (p. 570) say that in the Aru languages 'stress is not predictable', penultimate 'as a rule' but final in around 30% of cases, i.e. lexically distributed. Schapper & Zobel's statement is about the Aru group and cites Dobel, Kola and Batuley, not Ujir. Collins 1982 says nothing about Ujir stress. No Ujir-specific published phonological description of stress has been found in the compilation.
